about.what: Engine E4's own settings: what the national pathway model adds to prairieland.json, which it reads and never retypes. The plan's levers and their ranges, the operating settings of the existing fleet, the penalty costs that keep every run solvable, the tie rule, the presets and capstone C4's accounting inputs. Read by SB4 (learn/sb4-pathway-explorer.qmd), M13 (learn/m13-national-pathway.qmd) and C4 (learn/c4-prairieland-2050.qmd).
about.line: Prairieland is fictional; its numbers are illustrative.

dataset.creator: Honglin Li
dataset.status: Illustrative: engine E4's settings for fictional Prairieland (the levers and their ranges, the existing fleet's operating settings, penalty costs, the tie rule, the presets and C4's accounting inputs), set for teaching or derived from prairieland.json; the two stress hours come from SPP's 2025 hourly shapes (EIA-930).
dataset.source: Prepared for the course's engine E4, which takes every Prairieland number from prairieland.json and from this file only what the model adds; the stress hours (`stress`) are read from SPP's 2025 hours (town_year.json) by prairieland.json's hour rule.

nuclear.note: variable O&M of these existing plants, $ per MWh, set for teaching

existing.gasFromNew: Existing gas plants have the new plants' fixed and variable O&M (prairieland.json costs.technologies gasCC and gasCT) at their own efficiencies.
existing.fixedOM: Existing wind, solar and batteries have the new plants' fixed O&M (prairieland.json costs.technologies) for the model years they are still open. It is the same in every pathway (they run to their retirement years), so it moves no decision and no difference between pathways. The data give no fixed O&M for the existing hydro and the steady plants of Capital Valley: their upkeep is left out of the pathway cost. Existing plants' capital is sunk.
existing.set: teaching: availability factors stand in for outages (the planning model has none); coal and oil plants' fixed and variable O&M ($ per kW-year, $ per MWh) are illustrative

conventions.periodYears: Each model year stands for the five years that end in it (2030 for 2026-2030, ..., 2050 for 2046-2050): its yearly costs count five times, each year discounted to 2025.
conventions.online: A plant counts in a model year only if its retire year is later (prairieland.json capacityByYearMW), so it leaves the plan in the five-year period that contains its retire year: Plains Station, in service to the end of 2030, is out of 2026-2030; Ridge Station, to the end of 2037, counts in 2035, not in 2040. A conservative simplification: up to five years less of each retiring plant than the calendar gives.
conventions.newPlants: A plant built in a model year runs in that model year and in each later one its life covers; it pays yearly capital (an annuity over its life at the discount rate) and fixed O&M for the years it runs up to 2050. The payments after 2050 are its residual value, not charged.
conventions.fuels: Fuels are bought at the national level, at least cost. Gas comes from domestic fields (up to the 2025 output; 5% of it used in the fields) and LNG, in whatever mix costs least within the import cap: under a tight budget LNG can win, because the national inventory counts the gas burned in domestic fields but not LNG's upstream emissions abroad. Domestic crude (up to the 2025 output) goes before imported crude; crude goes to the refinery (5.5% lost) except what oil-fired plants burn; coal comes from Ridge County's mines (1.4% used at the mines), no imports. The full-year check buys gas in the same mix as the slice run of that model year.
conventions.firm: The generic firm clean option has no location: its output is shared among the regions in proportion to their demand, so the model never chooses where it goes. Its build limit is the generic 2 GW a region a period, for the five regions together (10 GW a period).
conventions.primary: Primary energy on the physical energy content method (prairieland.json balance.conventions): fuels as burned, existing nuclear as its heat (electricity / 0.33), hydro, wind, solar and the generic firm option at their electricity output.
conventions.electrification: A sector's fuel use switched to electricity rises in a straight line from 0 in 2025 to the plan's 2050 share; each GJ of fuel switched delivers its useful energy (prairieland.json balance.useful.efficiency) from electricity at the sector's ratio (demand.electrification). End-use equipment costs are left out, so the engine does not choose electrification: the plan does.
conventions.newLoads: New large loads (factories and data centers, loads only) are spread over the regions in proportion to their 2025 electricity use; straight-line between the years prairieland.json gives.

penalties.what: Penalty costs, never part of a reported cost: electricity not served ($10,000 per MWh), CO2 above the cumulative budget ($1,000 per tonne), imports above the cap ($100 per GJ) and a shortfall at a stress hour ($750,000 per MW a year, ten times a new gas turbine's yearly cost). They keep every run solvable. The budget and the cap are limits, not prices: a run that misses either at these penalties is solved twice more, for the least overshoot (with no more electricity unserved and no more stress-hour shortfall: serving demand comes first) and then for the least cost at that overshoot. A plan within reach is the least-cost plan within the limits, whatever their dual; a plan out of reach shows the closest pathway and by how much it misses.

tie.what: The tie rule (so that every reported number has one value): $0.05 per MWh carried on any link, $0.50 per MWh out of a battery, $0.01 per GJ more for imported crude than domestic crude; left out of every reported cost.

electrification.unit: electricity's share of the sector's useful energy in 2050 (%); it rises in a straight line from 2025's
electrification.set: teaching defaults; the ranges come from prairieland.json: from 2025's share to at most 15 points a period (75 by 2050), at most 100%, industry at most 60%

importCap.unit: % of primary energy, in every model year

mineralBan.what: A price shock on new plants meets the plants not yet bought: the plan's decisions through the model year before the shock are kept, and the shock year's new plants are re-planned at the shock's price. The other shocks meet plants already built: decisions through the shock's model year are kept, that year runs what was built, later years re-plan.

budget.why: E4's default plan: prairieland.json's default (2,600 Mt) is out of reach with the levers E4 has (the least any pathway reaches at the most electrification and central demand is about 2,700 Mt); the page shows the data's presets as marks on the slider.

reserve.what: The peak-hour reserve rule (teaching): at two stress hours of 2025's weather, the peak net-load hour and the busiest hour of the scarce-wind week, every region's load plus a margin must be met by plants at their availability, wind and solar at that hour's output, batteries at full power, the firm option's share and the links. The slices alone would let a plan lean on twelve-hour averages; adequacy itself is never judged here (lesson A5).
